title: The 10 Best Scroll Saws
subtitle: 16- to 22-inch variable-speed scroll saws for fretwork, puzzles, inlay and intricate curves, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: A scroll saw cuts tight curves and interior cutouts in wood, plastic and thin metal that no other saw can reach. We ranked 10 best-sellers on rating, review volume and features (tool-free blade changes, a work light, an upper arm that lifts for inside cuts and a throat of 20 inches or more). The throat size sets the largest piece you can turn: 16-inch saws suit hobby work, 20-22-inch saws handle big panels. They run from about $110 for Dremel's compact Moto-Saw to $900 for JET's 22-inch.
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

buyers_guide.q: What size scroll saw do I need?
buyers_guide.a: The throat (16, 20 or 22 inches) is the distance from the blade to the back of the arm, which limits how wide a piece you can turn. 16 inches handles most hobby work; 20-22 inches suits large fretwork, signs and panels.
Pinless blades are thinner and thread through tiny starter holes for fine inside cuts. Pinned blades are easier to change but need bigger holes. Most saws here take pinless blades; some take both.

buyers_guide.q: Why does a lifting arm matter?
buyers_guide.a: For inside cuts you drill a hole, thread the blade through, and reattach it. An upper arm that lifts and locks makes that quick, which matters on pieces with dozens of cutouts.
Most saws tilt the table for bevel cuts. Pro saws like the BUCKTOOL and JET tilt the arm instead, so the workpiece stays flat and easier to control.
Slower speeds for thin wood, plastic and metal (to avoid melting and burning); faster speeds for thick hardwood. Variable speed lets you dial it in.
